pr_contents:
Hi,

I propose this PR. Unfortunately It turned out being a little too "bulky".

1) I am working on a third solver based on qpOASES and to avoid errors and duplicated code, I propose to use a base class and to have ChainIkSolverPos_TL and NLOPT_IK inheriting from it.

2) Some minor cleanups. Here and there. In particular, I suggest a more consistent namespace and less copy and paste. I also prefer less cryptic names. 
I understand that this might occasionally fall into the "personal taste" field.  

3) A less misleading information from the benchmark test. Instead of informing the user of the average time including both successful and failed IK, inform only of the average speed of successful samples. This is IMO a less biased source of information, since it actually inform about the ability of the algorithm to converge.
pr_comments: May be this PR is too big, do you want me to split it in smaller ones?

The main problem is that I have private v2.0 that we've been using on a commercial project, and I've been hoping to find time to make public,  that probably won't be consistent with any of this.  If you make it smaller, it might make it easier for me to also sync the changes into v2.0.

Ok, I see. When are you releasing 2.0?

My main motivation for having a baseclass is to add other solvers, in particular [Ipopt](https://projects.coin-or.org/Ipopt), [qpOases](https://projects.coin-or.org/qpOASES) and [lma_kinematics](https://github.com/ros-planning/moveit/tree/kinetic-devel/moveit_kinematics/lma_kinematics_plugin)
Ideally I also would like to select which one I use at runtime (yaml file?)

Additionally, I would also like to be able to extend the API to allow underconstrained IK, i.e task that control only 3 DoF or 5 DoF (very common in my use cases).

Last but not least, it would be nice to add a secondary solver for redundant manipulation to find a solution that avoid singularities or reduces the amount of motion.

As you can see, I have a bold vision for this library ;)

The question is if we want to work together or if we have different goals or agendas.

1) the solver already allows underconstrained ik.  If you set the bounds to be large (or fltmax) that dimension becomes unconstrained.  That was kind of the point of the original work on this.

2) the manip-product condition already avoids singularities by maximizing manipulatity metric and pushing away from limits.

I feel like maybe you are trying to push the API on this without really understanding what is already there.  Perhaps bounds and conditions could be better documented.

1) Indeed, you are right. Forget what I said.
2) Inspecting the source code it is really hard to understand how this is done. APPARENTLY you just run the solver multiple times, using random seeds, until you get a timeout. 
This is a quite different from what I was thinking, i.e. exploring moving in the null-space of the first solution. Honestly, though, I have no data/benchmark to know which approach is more robust... yet ;)

Forgetting these two points, do you see any value in the ability to use different solvers? Which are the goals/improvement of 2.0, if I may ask?

On  point 2, you are correct.  That is what I am doing, and it is different from exploring the null space directly.  The issue with exploring the nullspace directly using the nonlinear optimization is that the null space criteria becomes the function to minimze and the final position becomes a constraint, but given the large search spaces of 6/7-DOF chains, this doesn't converge in any reasonable time.  So, you are back to doing typical Newton-style gradient descent like KDL.  I'm not saying this is bad, but its kind of different from the "style" of TRAC-IK.    Additionally, in version 2.0, there is also collision detection folded into the solver as well, which makes the traditional search using the null space even harder.  This is why I've stuck with the apporach of "find as many solutions as possible and then filter/sort at the end".  

I think the software could benefit from different solvers, but my plan for TRAC-IK was never a "Framework" to allow user to pick and choose at runtime.  Ideally, there would be a small, set number of solvers that have different benefits and advantages that run in parallel.  If we can show that new solvers improve the TRAC-IK solution rate even more (or reduce solve time), then I'm all for it, but I'd like it to just become the default state of the solver.  That said, it should be easier to swap in new solvers to do these tests -- either by substituting for one of the current two solvers, or to run together with them as a third solver.

v2 has a Cartesian trajectory generator that takes the non-collision goal IK, either min-distance or manip-product condition, as provides a "straight line" trajectory between the start and end poses that is guaranteed to not have joint rollouts and not collide with obstacles (currently only self collisions, but I need to add a "Planning Scene" like MoveIt! has).  This is all completely independent of MoveIt!, but eventually it would be nice to make it a MoveIt! "capabality" plugin that could replace the underwhelming Cartesian motion default in MoveIt!.

I'm excited about your enthusiasm in helping extend this.  Let's continue the discussion, and after this holiday week, I'll try to spend time next week at least getting a 2.0rc branch into the public repo for you to start examining.  Perhaps your Pull Request will merge in smoothly, but I suspect the header/API changed enough to where that isn't the case.
ok, I guess that for the time being I will just close this and wait for 2.0

pr_contents:
A new branch of ds\_asio is up for you consideration named 'blocking\_asio\_tests'.  As the name implies it enables blocking reads from DsConnection-derived classes with timeouts.  I have written a test named 'test\_serial\_blocking\_io' that works the solution from raw serial port file descriptors to boost::asio only interaction through the final ds\_asio-based changes.

This is a potentially large behavior change and I'd like people to review this before the changes are approved.  This does open up a way to block a process indefinitely if users are stupid.  However, the upside is that it greatly reduces the complexity of the traditional send/receive pair, for which we don't have a current async solution.

Like the serial port fixes from last week, this code is strictly linux-only and uses lower level calls that boost does not abstract.

Short summary of changes:

* DsConnection

    * changed 'receive' method to 'start\_async\_receive'
    * added 'stop\_async\_receive' method
    * added 'blocking\_receive' method
    * added 'native\_handle' method
    
* DsSerial

    * implemented 'stop\_async\_receive'
    * implemented 'blocking\_receive'
    * implemented 'native\_handle'
    * Added protected constructor to bypass parameter lookup
    
* DsUdp

    * implemented 'stop\_async\_receive'
    * implemented 'blocking\_receive'
    * implemented 'native\_handle'
    
* DsNodeHandle

    * removed call to ros::NodeHandle destructor in ~DsNodeHandle
    * Tagged raw pointers as possible memory leak

pr_title: WIP: adding logic for checking dvl beam quality metrics in deadreck loop
pr_contents: Still needs some simulation testing
pr_comments: Our metric for goodness is “if any beam quality value exceeds a threshold”?  Does this set us up for 4 “good flag” beams and only one beam quality > threshold still passing our test?

@{557058:c968e894-e5b2-481e-8f28-6ae245b00d5d} This block just checks for beam quality relative to the threshold and sets the good\_beam\_quality flag based on that. The if statement below \(copied here\)

```
if ((dvl_.getLast().num_good_beams > 2) && good_beam_quality && 


	  (fabs(dvl_.getLast().dvl_time - dvl_.getPrevious().dvl_time) < 10.0))
```

  
checks for num\_good\_beams > 2 and last dvl\_time < 10.0 in addition to the new good\_beam\_quality flag before deciding whether to integrate or not so I believe we’re covered.   
  
To successfully integrate dr from a new dvl message you need:   
1\. num\_good\_beams > 2  
2\. good\_beam\_quality = true  
3\. last dvl\_time - previous dvl\_time < 10.0 seconds  
  
If any of those conditions fails, it will trigger DVL\_HOLD status using last known velocities until the timeout kicks in and we switch to model velocities

@{5d2cea0498c0b10c5478ec8a} Right, I saw that and having a 3 term compound clause is it’s own subject I won’t start picking at.  

I guess my comment is more conceptual than about the implementation.  If this whole thing is motivated by the “good beams” flag not being actually representative of the number of good beams it just seems introducing another parameter called “good\_beam\_quality” and setting it true if one beam is good leads to the same misconception.

‌

@{557058:c968e894-e5b2-481e-8f28-6ae245b00d5d} Yeah good point on the compound clause, I was hoping to make the minimum amount of changes, but I don’t love it either. My analysis of the DVL failure dives from Boettcher/McDermott \(and a few other randomly selected ones with no DVL issues\) shows beam\_quality is basically either 0 or 254/255 for all beams. So I think this code should cover the edge case we’ve seen a couple times, but maybe worth discussing whether we want to use beam\_quality as a better indicator of the number of good beams and just remove the “num\_good\_beams” check altogether? We could check beam quality based on a preset threshold for each beam and then set our own num\_good\_beams indicator based on the beam\_quality field. Does that seem reasonable?

@{5d2cea0498c0b10c5478ec8a} The fact that there’s both a “num good beams” and “beam quality” metrics that can be wildly divergent is worth pinging RDI about.  We could then rework the logic based on their input and see what it would have done for the failures in Boettcher/McDermott

This is also a great case for unit tests to make sure these assumed behaviors work as intended..

@{5d2cea0498c0b10c5478ec8a} I’m also seeing the 0 vs 255 for the Tasman. But, the data from the engineering cruise shows the Nortek has beam quality metrics as a floating point number that is averaging around 0.01. Is that due to implementation on our end, or as reported from the Nortek? Does it make more sense to instead have a ‘trustworthy\_speed\_over\_ground’ flag and then move the logic for checking beam quality to each respective driver?

Update: this PR solves for the specific edge case identified on sentry758 and previous dives, but further investigation reveals that the num\_good\_beams metric itself is derived from beams where range > 0.25 which is pretty failure prone. In essence, we are only checking ranges and not whether those ranges are actually valid before attempting to deadreckon. At minimum, switching num\_good\_beams to be based on correlation would provide a better indicator. I am working with RDI to determine their preferred PD0 field for beam validity.

  roslaunch ds\_sensors spartonm2.launch serial\_port:="/dev/ttyUSB0"

Note: Much of the sparton driver code was pulled from an outdated, existing branch “dev-owttisubl”
